utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sojic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sojic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you to make a pause between questions and answers, because it's not easy for the interpreters, and we need everything to be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I see 1D6721 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement that you gave to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read through the statement and signed it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you here today, would the substance of your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender this statement into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to the associated exhibits, there are two listed and both are already admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the exhibit number for 1496?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, while there's no objection from the Prosecution, the Chamber notes that some -- some part of the para 23 relates only tu quoque evidence, not relevant to the indictment, so the Chamber will order to delete the part starting from "The first serious attacks on the Serbs in Pofalic, "to the end the paragraph. With that redaction, the Chamber will admit the 92 ter statement. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D6721 becomes Exhibit D2683. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would now like to read out a summary of Mr. Dragan Sojic's statement in English. [In English] Dragan Sojic was born on 10th of November, 1961, in Majur, Sabac municipality, Republic of Serbia. He completed secondary school for civil engineering and graduated from the faculty of architecture in Sarajevo. Having graduated, he worked as a trainee architect in the Dom design office in Sarajevo. Before the war, he worked at the secretary of the secretariat for urban development, housing and public utilities at the Novo Sarajevo municipality and was a member of the Executive Committee of the municipality, which is municipal government. Between late June 1992 and December 1993, Mr. Sojic was on the VRS defence line at the Jewish Cemetery in Sarajevo. In early 1990, the Muslims established the SDA followed by the Croats establishing the HDZ, providing the Serbs with a powerful motive to establish the SDS in July 1990. The work of the party was public and transparent and the decisions were taken in a democratic atmosphere. Dragan Sojic knew that the SDS policy was not to remove Bosnian Muslims or -- and Croats permanently from BH territory by means of genocide, persecution, extermination, killings, deportation, and inhumane acts. The SDS won in the Novo Sarajevo municipality. A coalition was created between the three parties. However, the SDS appointed a member of the SDA into the position of president as a sign of goodwill. The coalition operated well until the adoption of the decision of the independence on BH as the Serbs were out-voted and therefore the Assembly of the Serbian people in BH was constituted. A problem in Novo Sarajevo arose due to the sudden illegal construction of the many residential and other buildings in the municipality, which was replicated around Sarajevo. A large number of Muslims settled in these houses. However, the issue could not be resolved as there was no support from the Muslim part of the authorities. Dragan Sojic was aware of the military organisation and arming of the Muslims and Croats in Novo Sarajevo as he would see groups of Muslims hiding weapons under their jackets. He was also aware that they had their own Crisis Staff that organised the barricades in Sarajevo. Dragan Sojic knew that the Serbian Municipal Assemblies were established because the Muslims and Croats were preparing for war against the Serbs. Crisis Staffs in Serbian municipalities were formed and assumed all the prerogatives and duties of Municipal Assemblies when they were unable to convene. The commissioners of the staffs were tasked with trying to establish a rule of law in all Serbian municipalities. War Presidencies were established in municipalities because an imminent threat of war was declared and their task was to preserve the rule of law and normal life under these circumstances. The presidencies were not a means for the persecution and destruction of the citizens of Muslim and Croatian nationalities. Wartime commissions also existed, headed by republican commissioners to normalise life and meet the humanitarian needs in the territory. The city of Sarajevo was divided by the barricades, and this made it impossible for Dragan Sojic to travel to work. After these had been erected, inter-ethnic intolerance increased and Serbs locked themselves in their houses at dusk and gunfire could be heard coming from the direction of Muslim homes. The Serbian population organised themselves to stand guard at night and collect weaponry. The first serious attacks on Serbs began in May. Muslim units carried out attack --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: -- but it is redacted. I see. To Dragan Sojic's knowledge, there were no prisoner of war camps -- no prisoners or camps for prisoners of war or collection centres in Novo Sarajevo and no instructions were received from the organs of the Republika Srpska to organise any. Mr. Sojic was also not aware of any paramilitary units that existed in Novo Sarajevo. However, measures were taken -- control all those who were not official formations. At the beginning of the war in the chaos, looting, thefts, robbery and murder did occur. There was no discrimination on ethnic grounds when humanitarian aid was distributed. All citizens had access to public institutions but their freedom of movement was limited by the Muslim forces whose members were situated on a high-rise buildings and constantly using sniper rifles, shells, et cetera, and killed civilians who moved across exposed areas. A large number of civilians, including women, children, and the elderly were killed in this way during the war. In 1994, Dragan Sojic was president of the staff for the movement of civilians. This staff received requests from individuals to cross into Muslim-controlled areas and made a list of those whose requests were granted and sent them through SFOR, UNPROFOR, to the Muslim side for approval. This ensured conditions for the population to move safely from one part of the city to another. [Interpretation] That would be the summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I just have one comment to make in relation to the summary. I appreciate that they don't have evidentiary value, but the summary included the statement that Dragan Sojic knew that the SDS policy was not to remove Bosnian Muslims or Croats permanently by means of genocide, persecution, et cetera. What the statement actually says at paragraph 19, is: "I do not know - I have never heard that the civilian authorities at the regional or local level ... planned, instigated, ordered or assisted in the permanent removal...," and I think those are two quite different statements. And, again, I appreciate there's no evidentiary value, but these summaries are read out for the benefit of the public, and I think it's important that the public be given an accurate summary of the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sojic, I'd like to ask you about some possible corrections that cropped up in the course of the proofing note with the Defence team. In paragraph 7 you spoke about the change of the authorities in the Novo Sarajevo municipality. Could you tell us when Mr. Radan was elected as a member of the Municipal Executive Committee and when Mr. Prijic was elected to that committee.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in March the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo was established. That was a founding Assembly and not all the organs were elected there. Dr. Milivoje Prijic as the president was elected somewhat later, as well as Branko Radan as the president of the Executive Committee. They were elected at the following Assembly, at the following Assembly that was held in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 9, did you confirm in the presence of the Defence team that -- or, rather, according to your information, the SDS in Novo Sarajevo municipality, did it function in an independent manner, and what sort of links did it have, or what was the nature of the links that it had with the SDS central office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: The executive -- the municipal executive in Novo Sarajevo was in no way different from any others. The SDS functioned on democratic principles and that was also the case for the SDS in Novo Sarajevo. So it was fully autonomous when it had to take decisions within the Executive Committee, and this had certain implications for the officials appointed in the municipality itself. Paragraph 9, the claims there can be confirmed by me or supported by many examples that I could provide. If you remember, the office for revenue had to be -- belonged to someone else. The Municipal Committee of Novo Sarajevo had a decision that was different to the decision taken by the urban committee, so a woman remained working at that post. Her name was Dobrinka Gavrilovic. If I remember this correctly, that was her name. That's not the only example. Mr. President, if you remember this, when the president was elected to the Executive Committee, to the Executive Board, one of the candidates who tried to impose a member to the President was Asin Kubina [phoen], and he was fully appropriate according to his qualifications for that position, but the Municipal Board decided that Zarko Djurovic should be appointed to that post. And if you remember, we did not accept that -- we didn't want anyone to impose such a solution when it came to staff at the time. This concerned the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sojic. With regard to paragraph 24, could you tell us where you were, in which unit of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: When I returned from Montenegro, as it says -- it says in my statement why I left there. After Pofalici fell, after I lost my home, I had an invalid father. And my wife and mother, I took them to my sister, and I returned to Novo Sarajevo. So conscript, I reported there. I received an assignment. I was assigned to the 3rd Battalion, the 3rd Company of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. My commander, my company commander, was Mr. Slavko Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the nature of that unit? Was it a paramilitary unit? Were they volunteers? What sort of relationship did it have with the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: I was the only volunteer in that unit at that time, because I came from another part of town, from the right bank of Miljacka to the left bank of Miljacka. All the other people were inhabitants of Kovacici. I have Mr. Aleksic in mind, in fact. Before the war he worked for the post office in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he lived in Kovacici. So he stayed on to defend his home as did all the other men in the unit. It wasn't characteristic in any particular way. It wasn't special. Our company wasn't specific, apart from the fact that it was decisive and wanted to defend at any costs the population and property in Novo Sarajevo. We didn't want enemy units to be allowed to penetrate the Jewish Cemetery. As far as Slavko Aleksic is concerned and his physical appearance, because many people have associations in relation to his name, well, he's a man of exceptional qualities. He is an honourable officer, member of the military, and for private reasons, since I've known him I knew him a year or two before the war, he had long hair, a beard. I haven't seen him for a long time, but he still has the same appearance now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Mr. Aleksic close to the SDS at some point in time and at some other point in time to some other party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Slavko Aleksic, up until the beginning of the war was also a member of the Municipal Board or the local board in Kovacici, and when the war broke out, he put his work in the party on hold, and later he became close to the radicals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any information about certain criminals in your rear in Grbavica, behind your lines? Have you heard about Batko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've heard that name Batko. I'm not sure whether I know what his real name is, what his surname is. I have never seen him. But we weren't indifferent when we heard his name, because he is the way he was. He was a potential threat for all the inhabitants of Grbavica or Novo Sarajevo regardless of their ethnicity. To be quite frank, when my wife came from Montenegro, she was pregnant. It wasn't easy for me to be at the lines and to leave her alone. So it was with relief that we heard the news that spread rapidly amongst the soldiers that Batko was to be arrested and processed. I don't know what happened to him, but soon afterwards he disappeared and no longer showed himself in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 25 of your statement with regard to the blue routes, I'd like to ask you what these routes are, when they were opened and what the importance of these routes was.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: As a result of an agreement at the republican level and through the intermediary of the UN, the blue routes were opened to make it possible to move around freely. The Novo -- Novo Sarajevo was designated through their will as one of the destinations where the blue routes were to be opened up over the Bratstvo and Jedinstvo bridge. Since this was in our territory in the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo -- or, rather, the Serbian Municipality of Novo Sarajevo, its president appointed a staff for the movement of civilians. As a member of the civilian authorities I was also the president of the staff. The movement of civilians, and the staff consisted of the following: One of the members was a military security officer. Another member was the chief of the public security station, of the police station, in fact. There was also a member of the commission for exchanges was present. This was for the exchange of information. And I think that someone from the border police was also a member. Our role was the following: Citizens who wanted to visit another part of town, who expressed the wish to visit another part of town should submit a written request. We would examine it, and then through SFOR we had to send lists to the Muslim side and they did the same. People who received authorisation from the other side, because there were double checks, could cross over for a certain period of time from 12.00 or 2.00 to 4.00, I think. To be frank, that bridge didn't function every day. That connection didn't function every day because there were frequent incidents and fire would be frequently opened on the opposite side, and as a result that bridge would be closed for security reasons. If this is of any importance, we tried to act democratically. To the extent it was possible, we wanted to have an impartial staff working for the citizens, but on the Muslim side it was different, because our counterpart was the MUP, police -- a police body, and when we're dealing with freedom of movement, I don't think this is quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "visits," does that mean that some were returning and were there any requests for a longer term or permanent departure to the other side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: We did not receive requests that had to do with resettlement or choosing a place to stay. All the requests exclusively, because there was a section there, reasons for going, everybody would write visit to friends, visit to family, medical treatment, and so on and so forth, although there were cases that individuals from both sides when they were crossing would actually stay on the side that they would be visiting. More frequently it was the case that people would cross a number of times. I recall the Vjekoslava Sankovic, a professor who had an old mother in Sarajevo. She was a Croat. Some -- she crossed several times to visit her mother, to take her some food, medicines, and so on, and she wasn't the only such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 8, you talk about Crisis Staffs. Are you able to tell the Chamber when the first Crisis Staff was established in Novo Sarajevo and which party established it, and was there a special Municipal Staff of the municipality founded when it began to work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: The first Crisis Staff in Novo Sarajevo was formed by the Party for Democratic Action. After that, the Croatian Democratic Community formed a Crisis Staff and then while estimating or evaluating the security situation in the municipality, and I'm talking about this pre-war period because of some excess situations and the complexity of the situation and the fast developing events as a response to such a political security situation and in a way following the example of our neighbours, Croats and Muslims, the Municipal Board of the Novo Sarajevo municipality formed its own Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And at some point did the Serbian municipality form a municipal Crisis Staff and not a party Crisis Staff as an organ of power or authority, and when was this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Well, this was already at the time when we were instructed to form Crisis Staffs by the government. I cannot remember exactly the date, but I do know that in the functional sense, except for perhaps a couple of members of the previous Crisis Staff, the membership was the same as in the Crisis Staff that we already had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that you were at the founding session of the SDS, and then you talked about the coalition of these three parties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were you at the founding Assembly of the SDS on the 12th of July, 1990?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was St. Peter's Day, and this took place in Skenderija, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you recall who were the invited guests of our partners and who addressed the participants at the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Representatives of the other ethnic groups were at that Assembly, and sincerely speaking, the Serbian people on the whole were relieved after the Serbian Democratic Party was formed. Previously, the HDZ was formed, which was the pillar of the political power of the Croatian people, and then after that the Party of Democratic Action was formed. The Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina were expecting or awaiting to see what would happen with the entire Serb corps in the political sense. What made me particularly happy at this founding Assembly was when our guests, representatives of the other peoples, voiced their support for the establishment of the Serbian Democratic Party and at the same time expressed their resolve to remain in Yugoslavia, and this togetherness, which was a specific feature of Sarajevo, was a kind of hope that the winds of war partially due to the political will and because of what the representatives of the three peoples was saying would not engulf Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that was one of the reasons because when these issues were on the agenda, we were on the same wavelength. We formed a coalition and were fighting against the Communist rule from the previous regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D06722, please. It's a video-clip. We need to look at this in Sanction. 1D06722 from 0.54.47. It's not subtitled, but the interpreters have the transcript. 1D06722.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back a little bit to the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have a copy of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the beginning, and if possible can this interpreted to the participants.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] I invite and call Mr. Muhamed Filipovic to address the Assembly." Interpret's note: We do not have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I was just told that interpreters do not have the transcript. It's only one page I see from the e-court. Why don't we print it out and then provide them now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that this was already done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime while we are doing that, for the record, Mr. Sojic, it's at transcript page 11, line 24, could you tell us the name of the Croat professor who crossed the front line several times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was professor, Vjekoslava Sankovic, a woman who crossed the bridge several times to visit her mother who was elderly and ill in Sarajevo. I think she went only to visit her and to take her some food and medicines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked it because her name was not correctly reflected in the transcript. And while we are waiting, Mr. Karadzic, can we see the last sentence of paragraph 15 which reads, I quote -- shall we switch to Sanction -- no, no to e-court. End of paragraph: "The War Presidency was not a means for the persecution and destruction of the citizens of Muslim and Croatian nationalities." I noted that you also include this in your summary, but could you ask the witness what he meant by this statement, and in what context he said this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did you hear the question by His Honour?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: I heard the question, but I would like to see it on the screen, that part of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can we then look at paragraph 15, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Paragraph 15. Next page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, in both versions it's the following page. Can we zoom in a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This last sentence, what did you mean when you said that? What made you state this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: The previous assertion a couple of sentences before had a consequence of this conclusion that the War Presidency was not a means for the persecution and destruction of the citizens of Muslim and Croatian nationalities, because it was the duty of the War Presidency in imminent danger of war to contribute to the normalisation of the life of all citizens in the area of the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo. In view of the fact that we never discriminated or differentiated among the citizens by their ethnic affiliation, I felt that it was necessary for me to point out that the War Presidency was not a means to be used for the persecution or destruction of the citizens of Muslim and Croatian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And if this is a satisfactory answer, perhaps we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I'll leave it at that. Shall we continue with the video now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Allow me to welcome you on behalf of myself and on behalf of the organisation I am representing. I am pleased that after 50 years I can address you by your real name. To address you by your real name. Before, we were addressed as working people and citizens or this or that, and our names are historical names which directed our lives, to overcome various powers and charismas of our history were not legal and could not be mentioned in our political and public life. Let's hope that that is now the end of it, and I am extremely, extremely happy that I can greet you this way. "I would like to say also that we all felt a great relief in the fact that the Serbian nation in Bosnia and Herzegovina has decided to create and to express its political will in the way that it transpires from its nature and its own history. Be assured that we will respect your will and that between us there will be no anti-Serbian attitude. "This was not left to us by our forbearers. I do not want to talk now about a number of examples of mutual respect and consideration, but what I want to say and what is true without doubt is that we are people from the same creator, of the same qualities. We are people with the same language, we are on the same land with a common future, and it obliges us to make mutual agreements and to take care of each other, to take care of this common Bosnia and Herzegovina of ours and common Yugoslavia. "For that reason, I salute you, and I wish you a very happy beginning on this day, and even better continuation. Good luck."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember this address by Professor Muhamed Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Earlier when I was saying that as glad as we were that the SDS was formed, we were also very appreciative of the support of the officials from the other political parties of the other two peoples, and this -- what finally resulted in this coalition at the local level until it came to that part which Mr. Filipovic referred to as well, and that was the out-voting of the Serbian people, and it was a disregard for the will of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And -- thank you. And did Professor Filipovic stand by this commitment to preserve Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia, and was he the one who initiated the agreement between the Serbs and Muslims in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it wasn't only Professor Filipovic. It was the Bosnian Muslim political organisation at whose head he was. That idea of preserving Yugoslavia and unity in Bosnia and Herzegovina was present in the SDA party as well. The public is aware that even at key moments, Mr. Muhamed Cengic at one point in time as an expression of goodwill of the SDS [as interpreted] party's policy expressed his readiness and commitment for the survival within Yugoslavia and then a couple of days later Mr. Alija Izetbegovic forced him literally to lie and to make a strong turn against this common aspiration which then led to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you very much, Mr. Sojic. At this point I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 4, it should say SDA, SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we please -- I would like to tender this excerpt from the SDS Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it. Shall we give the next Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D6722 becomes Exhibit D2684. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sojic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief has been admitted into evidence in most part in writing in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sojic. I just want to start by clarifying --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Start by clarifying some details about your involvement in various organs at various times. At paragraph 23 of your statement, you said that after the erection of the barricades, you couldn't access the seat of the Crisis Staff in Lukavica, and you stayed at your house in Pofalici. And the barricades, they were erected in early March, I understand. So from early March your evidence is you could not access the seat of the Crisis Staff, and you stayed at your house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: No. No. It wasn't quite like that. The barricades which started to crop up in early March at different time periods were of different intensity and placed in different locations so that the daily situation dictated which part of the town would be passable and which would not. What is certain is that from April onwards, it was not possible to cross from one side to the other, because the Rad utility company, which was a local enterprise at the city level, and its director was Mr. Mirsad Kebo, a cadre of the SDA, put up heavy concrete blocks using machinery on the bridges which were in the Novo Sarajevo municipality. Now I'm talking about the area of Novo Sarajevo municipality. These blocks were placed on the Vodopriveda bridge, the brotherhood and unit bridge. So it was not possible, regardless of the security situation, physically to cross from one part of the city to the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So starting in March you had some difficulty accessing the seat of the Crisis Staff in Lukavica and from April onwards you were no longer able to access the seat of the Crisis Staff in Lukavica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So is it right, then, that from April onwards, you did not personally participate in the work of the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff or other municipal organs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: I cannot really recall not being able to cross to the other side, although I doubt it. It was too much of a risk to cross from Pofalici to Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So as far as you can recall, you did not personally participate in the work of any municipal organs from April onwards; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And then from the 16th of May to late June you were in Montenegro; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: No. On the 16th of May, I left Pofalici, crossing the Zuc Hill. From there with my family, and I mentioned earlier that my father was an invalid, I crossed to the Ilidza municipality because of the war actions in the area of the city. We stayed there for a few days. When the first opportunity appeared to transfer my family to Serbia, I did it from Ilidza. It was in a refrigerator truck. My wife, my mother, and my invalid father, we went into this refrigerator truck, and we went via Pale to Uzice, and then from Uzice we took the train to Bar. So this trek through Republika Srpska perhaps took four or five days. And then I came back in late June from Bar again through Serbia. I came back to Novo Sarajevo, and I reported for duty as a conscript when I was deployed to the line. From the beginning of my activities on the line, I was not a member of any Crisis Staff or any other body until the Novo Sarajevo municipality moved from Lukavica to Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when was that? When did the Novo Sarajevo municipality move from Lukavica to Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: I noted down the exact date here in my statement. If I could just look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we give the witness a hard copy of his statement, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At paragraph 25 of your statement you talk about becoming the president of a staff for the movement of civilians and humanitarian aid in early 1994. Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: No. No. I am thinking of December 1993. From mid-June until December 1993, I was a member of the Army of Republika Srpska, in the 3rd Company, the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. Although in view of the specific features of Novo Sarajevo and Grbavica, even after I left for work duty, it was my job that during any armed attack by the Muslim side I would be on the line of defence as a member of the VRS. Living in Grbavica at the time did not mean that you were automatically a member of the VRS or that you had to wage war. If you were assigned to work duty, then you were spared from the combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So basically from April, when you were no longer able to access the seat of the Crisis Staff, until mid-December 1993, you were not personally involved in the Crisis Staff or any other municipal organ; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And at paragraph 8 of your statement, you talk about the Crisis Staff. You say at paragraph 8: "Crisis Staffs in Serbian municipalities were formed based on the instructions of the government ... and the same was done in the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo." Those instructions D407 are dated the 26th of April, 1992. Now, today in your -- in answer to questions from Mr. Karadzic, you've referred to an earlier Crisis Staff established in Novo Sarajevo, a party Crisis Staff, and first I'd like to ask you whether you had any discussions with the Defence yesterday about this topic, about Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: As far as you can recall? It was yesterday. Did you have any --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: With the Defence? No, we did not discuss the Crisis Staff at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you said today that this party Crisis Staff that you were asked about was established following the example of your neighbours, the SDA and the HDZ, and you said following that example the Municipal Board formed its own Crisis Staff, but in fact that party Crisis Staff was established pursuant to instructions received from the SDS Main Board, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have P2575. You were a member of this party Crisis Staff, right, Mr. Sojic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: On your screen you will see minutes of a Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff meeting held on the 23rd of December, 1991, and in the first lines it says: "The meeting held on the premises of the Novo Sarajevo SDS heard and discussed the materials received from the SDS BH Main Board." And then it refers to the "First Degree," and then there are a number of items, and if you see item 3 it says: "Thirteen-member Crisis Staff established. Commander and his deputy appointed. And those instructions from the SDS Main Board which are in evidence as P5, say under item 3 of the "First degree," variant A: "SDS Municipal Boards shall establish immediately Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people in the municipality." And then it details the composition. So this document reflects the creation of a Crisis Staff in Novo Sarajevo pursuant to SDS Main Board instructions; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: No. As I have said previously, I explained the situation which resulted in the creation of the Crisis Staff in Novo Sarajevo municipality. If you look closely, just following item 3, it says that Mirko Sarovic and Dragan Sojic are appointed as coordinators for relations with the HDZ. So we were in charge of coordinating with the Crisis Staffs of the SDA and the HDZ. Otherwise, at any meeting of the Municipal Board, whoever was present during a Main Board meeting addressed this or that problem that was discussed there. What you can find in the minutes, which is that some documents were considered which originated from the Main Board. It is not easy for me to make a link between that and the initiative to set up the Crisis Staff. The reasons for creating the Crisis Staff were all around us in the field. It was the way we lived, the way things worked and this general danger that loomed all over the whole of Sarajevo. As members of the SDS, we deemed it necessary to establish a Crisis Staff. As I have explained already, by that time the other two national parties had already set up their Crisis Staffs and they were also taking part in sharing power with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, whether or not the other parties had set up Crisis Staffs and whether or not the local SDS was motivated to set up a Crisis Staff, it's right here in black and white: Thirteen-member Crisis Staff established pursuant to item 3 of the SDS Main Board instructions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: I don't see it on the monitor. I only see the document pertaining to the Crisis Staff meeting. You must be addressing an issue that can be seen in another document which I can't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: Did you ever see the 1991 instructions, the variant A and B instructions that the Chamber has received evidence and were being implemented in this document and in fact matches item for item that document? Did you ever see those instructions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: I responsibly claim that I have never seen the documents you mentioned, neither document A nor document B as you called them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to go now to 65 ter 01481.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But did you hear of the document? Mr. Sojic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And just following up on that, did -- at this 23rd of December meeting, you attended that meeting. The one that we see -- the document that was just previously on the screen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: The document you showed me is the minutes of a meeting of the Grbavica SDS local board on the 27th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I was talking about the previous document from the 23rd of December, the Novo Sarajevo SDS meeting. The one we looked at with the item establishing the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: That document --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you attend -- did you attend the meeting on the 23rd of December, the minutes of which we just looked at previously?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as you correctly noted we have minutes from a 27 of January, 1992, meeting of the SDS local board from Grbavica. And you see a list of people present numbered 1 to 12 and after that it says also present were Radomir Neskovic, Ranko Jugovic, Dragan Sojic and Bozidar Komad [phoen]. Do you recall attending this Grbavica local board meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could look under item 1, which is further to the bottom in the B/C/S and immediately under item 1 it says: "President of the local board Deyan Gutalj explained work of the Crisis Staff in the municipality." Then Cedo Miletic says: "I am interested in who has appointed members of the Crisis Staff and how come all of them are from the municipality?" And Deyan Gutalj says: "The Crisis Staff is formed according to SDS Main Board guidelines which precisely explain who is to be a member of the Crisis Staff." Now, this is another reflection of the fact that the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff was formed pursuant to the SDS Main Board instructions, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: I have explained what the motives were behind the setting up of the Crisis Staff in Novo Sarajevo municipality. As about this, you can inquire with Mr. Deyan Gutelj about this topic because I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Next exhibit, P exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 01481 becomes Exhibit P6066.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 7 of your statement, Mr. Sojic, you said that when the war broke out the part of the municipality that was controlled by the Serbs had to establish its government and so the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo was established on the 27th of March, 1992. This was a time when your evidence is it was difficult, at the very least, for you to access the seat of the Crisis Staff. So I'd like to ask you whether you had any personal involvement in the establishment of the Novo Sarajevo Serbian Assembly or municipality.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what was the extent of your involvement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: At the first multi-party elections I was the first person to be on the list of the SDS party for Novo Sarajevo municipality. The SDS won the elections, and I received by far the most votes. Not because I was someone who could mobilise 35.000 people, but simply because I was an SDS candidate. President Karadzic in his expose stated that it was a sign of goodwill. Irrespective of the fact that I was supposed to act as the municipal president, we handed over that position to the SDA and Mr. Kasim Demirovic became municipal press. As a member of the local government in Novo Sarajevo municipality and the secretary of the secretariat of our special planning and housing affairs, I had an important role to play in the functioning of the local authorities. That is why I was present when the Serb municipality of Novo Sarajevo was being set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And -- and when exactly was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: When what happened? I'm not clear about the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, it wasn't a very clear-cut question. The document establishing the Serbian Municipal Assembly is dated the 26th of March, 1992, although it was passed on the 27th of March, 1992. Were you actually present on the 27th of March -- 26th or the 27th of March when this document was drafted or when it was passed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: If you mean the Assembly session when the document was adopted, then my answer is yes. The founding Assembly meeting of Sarajevo -- Novo Sarajevo municipality and the making of the decision to establish an Assembly, that is when I was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And were you aware -- you explained that this was -- when -- you explained that this was done in response to the outbreak of war. The document, and this is D2675, the reference in your statement as I said is dated the 26th of March and was passed on the 27th of March, but war in Sarajevo broke out in early April, after this decision was passed; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: If you happened to be in Sarajevo at the time, I don't think you would put the same question to me today. I can use an example of mine, what it was like to go through an intersection next to the tobacco factory in Novo Sarajevo municipality. It was very difficult even in the period leading up to the war before Novo Sarajevo municipality was founded. As one went from the train -- tram stop to -- actually, as I went from the tram stop to my house, I came across a check-point controlled by the then official forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was very unusual. They stopped people and vehicles and asked for IDs. Doing so, they had long-barrelled weapons, which was not customary in terms of members of police who engaged in such task. When I was asked for my ID, I mildly protested because of the way they were doing it. One of the members of the police told me the following: If there wasn't anything that was clear to me he would take me to the staff to have it explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry to cut you off but your answers are very long and detailed and not specifically focused on the question. I understand from your answer that there were unusual situations like check-points. There may have been some tension, but you don't dispute the fact, do you, that fighting in Sarajevo actually broke out in early April?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, one could hear the firing of weapons even before the new year's, actually, quite before. There wasn't a single night in Sarajevo after dusk that one couldn't hear bursts of fire. When it dawned, everyone went to work tired because they didn't sleep, going and pretending that things went about as usual, avoiding to see or look at other people. It was in that kind of tension that we all lived in. As those in the party who were responsible --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's clear. Thank you. If I could ask you to focus your answers as much as possible. Okay. Were you aware that three days before the decision establishing the Novo Sarajevo Serbian Assembly was passed, the Republika Srpska had actually imposed that very dead-line of the 27th of March for the creation of Serbian municipalities in those municipalities which had not yet created them? And that's P961, page 24. Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: I don't see the document. I did hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not showing you the document. I'm just asking if you were aware of the fact that the Republika Srpska Assembly had imposed a -- okay. I see you're shaking your head. You were not aware of that dead-line. And were you aware that at that same --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Were you aware that at the same Assembly session on the 24th of March the Republika Srpska Assembly also verified the decisions of a number of municipalities which had already established Serbian municipalities, including the Sarajevo municipalities of Rajlovac and Vogosca? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: We had so many problems of our own that as regards the adjacent municipalities, we weren't all too curious. To tell you the truth, I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you talked about the fact that you joined Slavko Aleksic's company at the Jewish Cemetery in late June of 1992, and you said that that unit wasn't special in any way. The Chamber has received evidence that at the beginning of the war Mr. Aleksic led a group of volunteers referred to as the Novo Sarajevo Chetnik Detachment, and that's in P5035. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: I was not in Slavko Aleksic's company, as you put it. I was a member of the VRS, of the 3rd Company of the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. The commander of the company happened to be Slavko Aleksic. When I came to the line at the Jewish Cemetery the area of responsibility was just before us, and I fully -- and I will responsibly claim in that unit there wasn't a single volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was whether you were aware of the -- of the fact that at the beginning of the war, Aleksic led a group of volunteers known as the Novo Sarajevo Chetnik Detachment. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You referred to Aleksic's appearance, his -- the fact that he had a beard and long hair. That is typically associated with Chetnik appearance, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree. Quite the other way. His face looked enlightened. He was the kind of person that you would never detect anything evil or mean inside him, let alone him being a criminal.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I was talking about the hairstyle, Mr. Sojic. The beard and long hair, that's typical Chetnik appearance, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Quite the contrary. At certain points in time he resembled Moses.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you said that the unit you belonged to wasn't special in any way. I think those were your words. But it is true that Aleksic didn't have a regular VRS title or rank but referred to himself as a Vojvoda in military documents, a rank -- a title that was conferred on him by Mr. Seselj; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: It wasn't only Slavko Aleksic who came from the ranks of inactive officers of the VRS who commanded without having received any rank up to the level of battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But he -- he referred to himself as a Vojvoda rather than using any kind of military rank; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: I never heard him say that. He wasn't a person of authority in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: He was your company commander, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P5931, please. This is a 16 December 1993 request from Mr. Aleksic's company to the command of the 3rd Battalion requesting weapons and ammunition. And if we could go to the -- if we could zoom in on the signature and stamp at the bottom of the page. Now, that is a -- type-signed Commander Vojvoda Slavko Aleksic, and if we could zoom in on the stamp a little bit more. Now, that stamp, Mr. Sojic, reads "Sarajevo local commune board of the Serbian Radical Party," doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me what I can read on the monitor, then I say yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that Aleksic's -- that your unit was not special in any way, but would you agree that it would not be typical of the VRS -- of a VRS commander to sign a document with the title Vojvoda and stamp it with a Serbian Radical Party stamp? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, several questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this document is already on the screen, could we -- well, actually, could we have 65 ter 23872. While we are waiting for the document, Mr. Sojic, do you remember whether there was the rank of Vojvoda or duke as a rank of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: That rank did not exist, as far as I know. Well, to tell you the truth, I'm an architect, not an officer, but I've never heard of that kind of rank in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about any previous armed forces? Was it more of a honourary rank or title?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Due to the great successes of the Serb army in World War I, it adopted a number of ranks and titles. That is where the title of duke was assigned to brave men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the fact that some units followed in the tradition of long ago units carrying the name such as, for example, the 32nd Partisan Division and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at the document before you and tell us what it's about. Who are these assets being given to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: The document is dated the 19th of August, 1992, when the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps sent certain assets to the Koran command and authorised Dragan Vucetic and Slavko Aleksic as the persons who were supposed to take those assets over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of formation were these authorised representatives members of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: They were members of the 3rd Company of the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. Dragan Vucetic acted as commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So when you joined them, it went under that name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and not only then, but all the way until the end of the war. That unit actually was never disbanded. We remained at the location of the cemetery in Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 23872 shall be assigned Exhibit D2685. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have P6066 next. It was admitted today. Page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sojic, please have a look at the conclusions. For example, conclusion number 1, as well as number 5 and 14. Did the Crisis Staff and the local board act autonomously, and did they receive any instructions? In other words, what is it that they are asking for in this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: As for this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before -- before you answer, Mr. Sojic. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was wondering how it arose from the cross-examination, but -- could you reformulate your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sojic, this document -- on the first page of the document, it was suggested to you that the Crisis Staff of the local commune was working in accordance with instructions received from the party.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That wasn't -- that wasn't the proposition that was put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think -- the question was whether the Crisis Staff, local Crisis Staff was established pursuant to the instruction from the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, the municipal Crisis Staff. Now, there's some confusion that there's a Crisis Staff of the local commune. I never made any such suggestion to the witness. So this is confusing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at conclusion number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what conclusion number 5 relates to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: This document concerns two issues, Mr. President. First of all, it is about the autonomy of the local commune when it comes to its work because you can see from the discussions of all those who were present that they were fully informed of what took place at the Municipal Board. There are various conclusions, that there's a link with the Main Board, and so on and so forth, that they heard this and that. As a result these conclusions were drawn, and at the same time all of this is the result of the situation in Novo Sarajevo municipality, in the local commune of Grbavica, as a result of the situation in Grbavica. Under 5 it says convene a session of the SDS Novo Sarajevo and they are supposed to discuss the work of the Municipal Board there, the autonomy of the Municipal Board of SDS is present in relation to the local board. It's a revolt of the local commune of Grbavica, the local board of Grbavica, and as a result of this these conclusions were drawn. Under 14 it says specify activities of the Crisis Staff and the SDS Municipal Board. If there were any instructions here, if they had been applied, then they wouldn't have been afraid. They wouldn't have been concerned about what the work of the Crisis Staff was and about what the work of the Municipal Board was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now see P -- P2575. P275. P2575. When you're answering questions today put to you by the Prosecution, you said that the Crisis Staff wasn't established in accordance with these instructions that were issued on the 19th of December. Could we have a look at the date when this meeting of the Crisis Staff was held.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: The 23rd of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have a look at the top. Was this the founding meeting of the Crisis Staff, or was this one of the meetings in a series?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: This was just one of the meetings. The Crisis Staff was formed a lot earlier on, because this is in the month of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It won't take long, your Excellencies. [In English] If you're wondering how long, no, no it's not going to be long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Quite extraordinary, Mr. Karadzic, but do carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked -- or, rather, where were the headquarters of the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of all three political parties that participated in the establishment of the authorities in Novo Sarajevo was in the building of Novo Sarajevo. As parliamentary parties we had our own premises. For the purpose of good neighbourly relationships, at the beginning, these offices were next to each other initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In March did you go to the Novo Sarajevo municipal building in March to work there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where was the Crisis Staff of the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff of the SDS was established in the Novo Sarajevo municipality and our premises but it wasn't possible to continue functioning because one couldn't gain access to the municipal building in Novo Sarajevo. So it started working in premises elsewhere, not in the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know when the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established? When was its existence declared?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: I think it was in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not the Assembly, the republic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I remind you, would it be on the 9th of January?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: Shame on me. It's a bad day. Or, rather, St. Stephen's Day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did Republika Srpska start functioning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: It was only after the war had broken out that it started functioning, after the beginning of the war, because in the founding decision, the decision to found the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo, in one part of that decision we took account of the fact that war shouldn't break out, and therefore the officials from the SDS were responsible to perform their duties conscientiously and in accordance with the law. Only if the situation, the political and security situation, deteriorated, only if work broke out, was it going to be necessary to work in accordance with the decision on the establishment of the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I just didn't see how these last two questions arose from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: True, but I thought you were coming to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask Mr. Sojic whether the date on which the municipality or the republic was declared was also the date which they were founded or started functioning.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my last question: You were asked about when the war broke out. Do you know what took place on the 1st of March in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of March in Bascarsija in Sarajevo, a Serbian best man was killed, Mr. Gardovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what happened on the 3rd of March in Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SOJIC
utterances.text: The legal armies, Croatian armies, moved over into the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber needs to rise very soon. If you need to continue, we will have a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, your Excellency. That's fine. I just wanted to ask the witness about the agreement, but everything is fine. Thank you, Mr. Sojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.text: Then we'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 10 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For this session and tomorrow, we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Morrison being away. Yes. Good morning, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Your Honours, I just wanted to address a couple of the exhibits before the witness came in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can focus on paragraphs 65 through 73, please. This is -- this lists a number of associated exhibits. And there's only one other paragraph, Mr. President, and for that if we can look at paragraph 86. That is a document that I understand is a newspaper report. I could not find an English translation. I may be wrong about that. But from just reading the description here, it says the witness says I confirm the allegations in this document that Muslims attacked the company Zrak. utterances.text: Who will respond to Ms. West's submission? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since we have some time today -- before that, do you like to reply, Ms. West? If not, we'll carry on. Shall we go one by one in the order of the filing. So we'll not admit 1D8445 but admit only one, 8445A.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, perhaps it could be placed under one number. Both of them could be placed under one number, and then you might know where the entire map is. So it could be one exhibit. We could have both of these documents as one exhibit. It hasn't been correctly interpreted. My suggestion is that the Chamber is able -- so that the Chamber can see where the location is in the wide area, that we could have two exhibits attached and just one number assigned to those two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's take a look. Shall we upload 8445A first. Okay. And then this is with A. Can we see the map without A? We know where it is. It's part of -- let's take a look --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's sufficient, your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- at the larger map. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. It's sufficient to admit only 455 -- 8445A. And then I'll consult with my colleagues as to the exhibit raised by Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As regards the -- the exhibit referred to in paragraphs 65 to 73 will be received by the Chamber. We agree it's relevant to his case and forms part of the indispensable and inseparable part of the statement. That being said, we'll bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sure the Chamber knows, but this witness will require an advisement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujasin. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the accused, the Prosecution, or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal still then may compel you to answer the question, but in such a case the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel Vujasin.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please wait, both of us, between the question and answer so that the interpreters could have enough time to interpret everything and for everything to be recorded in the transcript. Sir, Colonel, did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement that you see in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Up until four, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you need to see the whole document, and do you need to have a hard copy for you to use? Do you have a hard copy in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: No, I don't have a hard copy, but I do have paragraphs 1 to 4 here on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please provide a hard copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we can print out and provide to the witness. In the meantime, shall we proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.text: Yes. The statement that I gave, I read it back and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
