utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this statement and the documents that can just go in without live testimony. After reading the summary, I would like to deal with some documents with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit the 92 ter statement first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 1D6723 shall be assigned Exhibit D2686. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll deal with the associated exhibits after his testimony is concluded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to read the summary of Colonel Vujasin's statement in English. [In English] Colonel Mihajlo Vujasin was born in Sokoliste, Bosanski Novi municipality, on 1st of March, 1955. He completed the military academy in Belgrade and was discharging the duty of company commander and chief of engineers at the Rajlovac airforce base. Mihajlo Vujasin was commander of the 1st Battalion at Rajlovac airforce base. After the war broke out, he became deputy commander of the Rajlovac brigade. On 16th of September, 1992, he was appointed chief of engineers of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Before the beginning of the shelling, the recruitment of personnel for the airforce base war units had been carried out on a voluntary basis and two units had been formed by Serbian volunteers and one by Muslims. The first shell hit Rajlovac in the evening on 4th of April, 1992, injuring about a dozen of cadets who attended training at the Rajlovac airfield perimeter. The shelling continued for about half an hour, targeting housing facilities and the command, among other. The position from which the shells were launched was inhabited strictly by the Muslim population. From that moment, non-Serbian JNA officers began to leave. Following the attack, the Butmir airfield was occupied by JNA units from the Rajlovac airfield. The JNA was responsible for securing the Butmir airfield in the event of emergency situations. The ethnic majority in Rajlovac was Serbian. The Territorial Defence at the time was majority Serbian since the Muslims did not respond to mobilisation calls. On 13th of May, 1992, the base was moved to Belgrade and the Territorial Defence took over the barracks in Rajlovac on 10th and 12th of May, 1992. The Territorial Defence consisted of locals from Rajlovac, Reljevo, Recica, and Zabrde settlements who had responded to mobilisation calls and refugees from Central Bosnia. The Territorial Defence members formed the Rajlovac Brigade at their own initiative without orders of the superior command, with the main aim to protect the population and property in Rajlovac. The task assigned by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps concerning Sarajevo was to retain the positions, not to enter the town, and to prevent the Muslim forces from breaking out of the town and linking with the Muslim forces on the outer ring. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps mostly defended itself. There were operations involving the improvement of tactical positions and those involving prevention by which the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps force, the Muslim forces to regroup and to use their resources. While carrying out combat operations firing or responding to firing from the town, neither he nor his brigade considered those operations as part of a systematic or widespread attack against civilians. The Rajlovac Brigade took precautionary measures to avoid firing on civilian facilities in the zone of responsibility of his -- of the opposing units. Also, when carrying out combat operations and firing on military targets in civilian zones, they took measures to reduce collateral civilian casualties and always warned the enemy through the corps command. The training level of the members of his brigade was initially poor but improved with time. The sabotage -- the shortage of professional staff influenced the quality of management, command and control. There were problems with ammunition, and they were always short of it, particularly of artillery ammunition. They had no knowledge that the task of snipers was to shoot civilians in the town controlled by the Muslim authorities, but he did know that there were snipers in the 1st Corps of BH Army targeting their own positions and civilians. His brigade was never ordered by superior command or civilian authorities, orally or in writing, to carry out attacks against civilians or means of public transport. Likewise, he never issued such orders. Neither he nor subordinates or superior commands had any intention of causing civilian casualties or terrorising or exerting psychological pressure on civilians under Muslim control. Conversely, Rajlovac was shelled in the depth of its territory, and Muslims -- Muslim shelling and sniper fire were frequent and civilian casualties in the zone of responsibility of his brigade were high. Muslim forces also forced civilians to dig trenches and fortifications towards unit of Colonel Vujasin's positions. There were various paramilitary groups raiding through Rajlovac with mercenary aims attacking victims indiscriminately and causing problems for both Serbs and Muslims. Superior command endeavoured to resolve this problem by disarming and expelling them or placing them under a unified command individually, not as units, and only those individuals who had not committed a crime. Orders stated that the attitude towards the UN members and civilians must entail full respect of the Geneva Conventions and abiding by the norms of the law of war. General orders and instructions received from superior command were that fire was to be opened against standard and established firing and combat positions and only when their own Serb positions were to be defended. From April 1992 to December 1995, the 1st Corps of BH Army was stationed in the town of Sarajevo controlled by Muslim forces. They had positions in dominant elevations -- elevated points in the -- in and around the town controlled by Muslim authorities as well as in civilian zones and buildings and in the depth of their territory. The unit of Colonel Vujasin had information about the existence of criminal groups in the 1st Corps of BH Army. Humanitarian aid went through Rajlovac unstopped. They had knowledge, however, about the misuse of humanitarian convoys for military purposes of the -- by the -- of the Sarajevo -- of the 1st Corps of BH Army. Most of humanitarian aid ended up with the units of these -- with the units of -- with soldiers of these units rather than the civilians. The Serbian side enabled the civilians to leave the town with the assistance of UNPROFOR, while the -- there were Serbian civilians in the town under the control of Muslim authorities who were not allowed to leave the town. They were informed, Mr. Vujasin and his own colleagues were informed, that Radovan Karadzic's stance was to enable full and unobstructed supply of humanitarian aid, water, electricity, and gas to civilians in the Muslim part of Sarajevo. Mr. Vujasin learned about the existence and production of modified air-bombs for ground targets during the testing of one such aerial bomb in Nisici. He has no knowledge of the existence of fuel air-bombs in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps arsenal. In the initial period of the war, they had poor relations with the local civilian authorities due to the latter's unrealistic expectations from the brigade and they demanded more that what the brigade was able to do -- than what the brigade was able to do. He did not have information of a Serbian municipal policy of persecution, killing or discrimination based on religious or ethnic ground in his brigade's zone of responsibility. [Interpretation] That would be the resume -- summary, and would I like to look at a few documents now and some paragraphs that need to be covered live.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Mr. President, if I can just make one comment [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before doing so -- yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for interrupting. I just -- a clarification and Mr. Karadzic will tell me if I'm wrong, looking at paragraph -- excuse me, page 49, and it's the last few lines, this is when Mr. Karadzic was summarising the information on snipers. And he said, summary, that he had no knowledge of the task of snipers was to shoot civilians in the town controlled by the Muslim authorities, but he, the witness, did know that there were snipers in the 1st Corps of the BH Army targeting their own positions and civilians. I just want to be clear this is from paragraph 43. When it says targeting their own positions and civilians, that appears to be the Bosnian Serb positions, not their own, meaning the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: That's completely right but just a mistake in the summary which is not, as I understood, which is not in evidence. But it's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at paragraph 61 of Colonel Vujasin's statement. We will not be using the interview of Mr. Bozic that we referred to before. The information in paragraph 61, is that something that you're aware of even without the interview?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We would like to keep paragraph 61.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you are not tendering that 17258.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, your Excellency. We showed it once and it was not admitted even though that's the interview of the late Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would just like to draw your attention to paragraph 86. We are not going to be using this document either, but I would like to ask you whether you know of this information even without the document and whether the information is correct. You were thinking of paragraph 86; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned that two brigades of volunteers were formed, two Serbian ones and one Muslim brigade, are you able to explain to us when this happened?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: I am talking about two units, not two brigades. Excuse me, Mr. President. Based on the task of the JNA at the time, the response to the call-up was not very good as far as both Serbs and Muslims were concerned, so there was a law adopted so that war units could be formed on a voluntary basis for the needs of the JNA, and then the Serb side formed two units, and the Muslims formed one unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the JNA armed all of them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes. It armed all of them, but later this had negative consequences in terms of the policy and the civilian structures of the municipality of Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Before we get into a role, I would just ask Mr. Karadzic to think about the questions he's asking and have them not be so leading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. This is in the statement, so all I wanted to do was to check something about these attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the question could be: Did you arm those three units without any difference, without differentiating among them?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And this was done before the 4th of April, before the attack on the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but he's just done it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's particularly difficult when we already admitted the statement and then -- but even if that is the case, please refrain from making a leading question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completely accept any objection, and I will do my best to learn to abandon the habit that I have formed over the past two and a half years when I did have the right to put leading questions. Excellencies, we would like to keep paragraph 86 but leave out the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just note that without this document, I -- the last sentence in that paragraph has no probative value at all. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, the Muslim forces of the 1st Corps, did they carry out any offensives against the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and were they successful in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes, they did carry out offensives, and they were successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D8406, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the document refers to paragraph 73 of your statement. Can you please tell us what this document is about? When was it drafted and what does it talk about?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Can you please zoom in? It's difficult for me to read. Yes. I was duty operations officer in the command of the RSK and there was a lot of combat at the time and only some skeleton staff were left at the corps command. Everyone else was in the field including General Milosevic and his assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the result was of those attacks and why this order? Why was it submitted through you to Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: That was the system of command. He had to go in the field so that he would personally be present in order to assist in keeping those positions. We tried to keep those positions because we were in a worse position than the enemy, and we tried to stabilise the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of successes did the Army of BiH achieve? What was lost? Line three.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: It is a village called Mosici which was trig point 929. By that time it had probably fallen, and this is what was reported. That was the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell something about the date for the sake of the Chamber? What was this part of?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: This was in June 1995, on the 21st of June. That's when there was an offensive on the Serb positions, I think in the entire Sarajevo theatre, but in this area they were the most successful, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit it as next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 1D8406 shall be assigned Exhibit D2687. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellency. At this point I have no further questions of Colonel Vujasin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I take it you are not tendering document 65 ter 7129, referred to in para 84, and 1D3259, the English translation of which is missing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, it has to do with the hand-over of the airport by the JNA to the civilian authorities, and then the civilian authorities handed it over to the VRS, but it's not that important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Eighty-six. It is -- so we will not tender documents 84 and 86.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then the remainder of the associated exhibits will be admitted and be given numbers in due course by the Registrar. As notified, we will have the cross-examination tomorrow morning. Mr. Vujasin, we will adjourn for today and continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. In the meantime, I would advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 20th day of December, 2012, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
